_about: Data for /research/page-errors (#5613), the companion paper to /research/quality. Classes, strata and presence counts are copied from .claude/docs/page-error-taxonomy.md (the 2026-09-25 by-eye study; per-book notes in scripts/eval/results/page-error-taxonomy-2026-09-25/findings/). Counts are PRESENCE: the number of books, of six drawn per stratum, in which a class was seen on at least one page of the pair. They are not rates. 'mech' is the mechanism (1-7, 0 = none of the seven); 'placed: true' marks a class the taxonomy did not assign to a mechanism and this paper did. 'detect' is the state of our instruments on 2026-10-02, checked against scripts/lib and scripts/audit on main. Specimens: every scan crop was opened and read on 2026-10-02 ('read from image'); crop boxes are in the image's own pixels; served text was read from the production database on 2026-10-02 (the I1 specimen from page_revisions, as served until 2026-10-01). Rights were checked against books.image_source.rights_normalized and the source for every crop; two Internet Archive microfilm scans with no named holder were left out. Segment kinds: same; wrong = served, but the scan shows something else; missing = on the scan (or in the source) and absent from what was served; invented = served, with nothing on the leaf behind it.

strata.name: Dense prose, 1500–1799
strata.drawn: at least 2,600 reading characters, printed, one column

strata.name: Two or more columns
strata.drawn: the OCR tagged both pages as two or more columns
strata.found: Only 2 of 6 are real two-column pages; the rest are unsplit spreads or strips of the facing page tagged as columns.

strata.name: Manuscripts
strata.drawn: the OCR tagged the script as handwritten
strata.found: Two Tibetan pecha boards, Gurmukhi, an English secretary hand, a photographed Maya and Spanish manuscript, Latin textualis.

strata.name: Short pages
strata.found: Mostly not short. The length field ignores tags and junk; one "108-character" page holds 8,100 lines of the character |.

strata.name: Plates and diagrams
strata.drawn: page typed illustration, plate or diagram
strata.found: Five real plates, and one text page with a wrong type that turned out to be one leaf away from its text.

strata.name: Music
strata.found: 2 of 12 leaves carry staff notation; no tablature, no underlaid text. Also astrology and a Psalm commentary.

strata.name: Tables and indexes
strata.drawn: index or table type, or a markdown table in the OCR
strata.found: As intended, plus a Syriac grammar paradigm and a hieroglyphic dictionary.

strata.name: Greek
strata.found: 2 of 6 are manuscripts catalogued as prints; 2 are parallel-text editions.

strata.name: Hebrew, Arabic, Syriac, Persian
strata.found: Four manuscripts and one Syriac and French edition; no Rashi script, no rabbinic-Bible layout.

strata.name: Chinese, Korean, Tibetan
strata.drawn: catalogue language Chinese, Korean or Tibetan
strata.found: Three Chinese woodblock prints, two Korean books, one Tibetan pecha board.

strata.name: Incunabula, 1450–1500
strata.found: One is a manuscript; one is a Suetonius catalogued as a German prognostication.

strata.name: Print, 1800–1899
strata.found: Three English books, plus Yoruba, Greek and lithographed German.

links.leaf: the image shown is the leaf transcribed
links.display: the reader is shown what was stored
links.record: the catalogue and derived fields describe the book

mechanisms.title: The model reads what it expects, not what is there
mechanisms.text: Faced with a hard or unfamiliar leaf, the model writes a fluent page in the right language and genre: a remembered canonical text, a normalised spelling, a confident expansion of an abbreviation. The translation then turns weak or invented source into fluent English, and notes explain misreads with invented learning. This is the largest family. It cannot be seen from the English alone, and the instinct that makes the model a good reader is the one that makes it a confident fabricator.

mechanisms.title: The page unit is not the leaf
mechanisms.text: Unsplit spreads, a strip of the facing page in the frame, three palm-leaf folios on one board, an image one leaf away from its text, a Hebrew book with its pages in reverse. The OCR transcribes a unit that has no single reading order, and everything downstream inherits the confusion.

mechanisms.title: Page furniture and apparatus have nowhere to go
mechanisms.text: Running heads, catchwords, signatures, block-hearts, footnote anchors, marginalia, interlinear glosses, plate labels, tables, a later reader's marks. Our page format has a handful of tags for these. The model assigns them wrongly, and the renderer trusts the assignment.

mechanisms.title: The seam
mechanisms.text: Catchwords, words split across the page break, and what the translator does with the last clause of a page. Around 30 of the 78 breaks we read had a defect. The harm concentrates there.

mechanisms.title: Two texts on one page
mechanisms.text: Facing or interlinear translations, a Latin crib beside the Greek, a Greek quotation inside a Latin commentary, an English source that needs no translation. The pipeline assumes one source language and one target. Where that is false it translates the crib, blends both, translates both, drops one, or paraphrases English into worse English.

mechanisms.title: Self-reported tags are trusted downstream
mechanisms.text: The model's own guesses about a page's language, script, columns, page type and page number are read as facts by routing, search filters, sampling, the language attribute a screen reader speaks, and our own page-integrity detectors.

mechanisms.title: The display contract is not enforced at write time
mechanisms.text: Unknown tags, broken tags, a whole translation wrapped in a metadata tag, reasoning left in the transcription. Each is stored as written and reaches the reader.

mechanisms.title: Outside the seven
mechanisms.text: Ordinary translation faults with a correct transcription, a translation cut short, two panes made from different reads, and metadata derived from bad text. They are listed here so that the count is complete.

classes.name: Image one leaf away from its text
classes.sees: The scan beside the text is the previous or next page. The transcription's own page number disagrees with the folio printed on the image.
classes.instrument: Image-hash alignment check (page-alignment.mjs); a second read of the page flagged all 7 known cases in the quality study. The cheaper page-number check was not run on these books.

examples.label: Ray, History of Hindu Chemistry, vol. 2

classes.name: Duplicate scan, back to back
classes.sees: The same leaf twice in a row; the OCR reads it twice.
classes.instrument: Duplicate-scan check in the page-integrity audit (20 of 20 confirmed by pixel correlation).

classes.name: Spread not split
classes.sees: Two printed pages in one image. The text holds one of them and the other is lost, or both are tagged as two columns; the translator sees the facing half and describes it.
classes.instrument: Spread detection at import catches most printed spreads; microfilmed openings and right-to-left books are split late or backwards.

classes.name: Strip of the facing page read as content
classes.sees: A "second column" of half-words beside the real text, sometimes translated into a list of English stubs; or the line openings rebuilt into fluent invented Latin.
classes.seenNote: 8 books had a strip in the frame; it was mishandled in 7.
classes.instrument: None. A two-column tag on a one-column page is the tell.

classes.name: Several leaves in one photograph
classes.sees: Three loose Tibetan folios on a board shown as one page; the next image holds their three versos, so page to page is not a reading order. The OCR mixes or duplicates the leaves.
classes.seenNote: Every Tibetan book in the sample.
classes.instrument: Where the stored text carries a leaf-break marker the translator keeps the leaves apart; 76,333 cohort pages had no marker on 30 September 2026.

examples.label: mDo sde brtags sna rgyas pa (Tibetan)

classes.noSpecimen: The British Library's statement for these scans forbids further copying, so no crop is shown.

classes.name: Pages in reverse order
classes.sees: Page 16 is the page before page 15; the catchword of 16 opens 15.
classes.instrument: Catchword-boundary check in the page-integrity audit. It catches this cheaply and was not run on this book.

classes.name: Catalogue identity or format wrong
classes.sees: A "1561 print" that is a manuscript; a "Prognosticon for Leipzig, 1490 [German]" whose leaves are a Latin Suetonius with commentary. The OCR's own script tag contradicts the record.
classes.instrument: None for format. The OCR's script tag against the catalogue is a free check.

classes.name: Confabulation on an illegible or unfamiliar leaf
classes.sees: A fluent page in the right language and genre that is not on the leaf: a treatise on divine simplicity where the leaf is a list of remedies. The translation renders it faithfully and the summary confirms it.
classes.instrument: A second read of the page finds some garble; a check for described pages catches only the polite version. No check anchors the text to visible words.

classes.name: Text in the wrong script
classes.sees: Devanagari Sanskrit ("Homage to Shri Ganesha…") on a Tibetan biography.
classes.instrument: A book-level audit of page scripts against the catalogue language (#4766) would catch this book; the affected Tibetan cohort is being re-read by a dedicated engine.
classes.noSpecimen: British Library scan; its rights statement forbids further copying.

classes.name: A remembered standard text put in place of the leaf
classes.sees: For a famous text, lines that are not on the leaf and lines on the leaf that are missing: the model recites the version it remembers.
classes.instrument: None. A translation much longer than its transcription on a well-known text is the tell.

classes.name: Repeated blocks
classes.sees: The same phrase or paragraph over and over, faithfully translated: "and the secret of the Shekhinah and the secret of the Shekhinah…" for 3,500 characters.
classes.instrument: A repeated-block check in the page-integrity audit (added after the study); the older word-variety ratio catches only word-level loops.

classes.name: Silent omission inside the page
classes.sees: Nothing, which is the point. A clause, a line or half a column is gone with no marker, and the sentences either side are fused into one fluent false sentence.
classes.instrument: A check for words the page's own vocabulary list names but its text lacks (added after the study). Most omissions leave no such trace.

classes.name: A misread that changes the meaning, carried into fluent English
classes.sees: A plausible sentence that is wrong: the saint becomes the patient, by-laws become land, sin becomes life throughout a page. Never an uncertainty marker.
classes.seenNote: It concentrates at ligatures in Aldine Greek, long s, abbreviation marks in incunabula, minims in textura, Fraktur, every cursive hand, and single characters in Chinese.
classes.instrument: None from text alone. Only a reading against the image finds it.

classes.name: Numerals, dates, doses and units
classes.sees: 190 soldiers become 150; five years become "[several]"; a dose of two drachms becomes three; Chinese place-value numbers that cannot be recovered from the English.
classes.instrument: None. A check that every number in the English traces to the transcription is free and not built.

classes.name: Silent normalisation toward the expected
classes.sees: The corrupt reading an editor quotes in order to correct it, silently corrected; variant spellings replaced by standard ones; a grammar's forms swapped for textbook forms; abbreviations expanded without a mark.
classes.instrument: None.

classes.name: Conventions flip between adjacent pages
classes.sees: Nothing on one page. Across a break: long s kept, then turned into s, then into f; diplomatic, then expanded; vowel points on one page of an edition and not the next. Search and quotation break.
classes.instrument: None.

classes.name: A second script on the page dropped or garbled
classes.sees: The Greek inside a Latin commentary replaced by other Greek or absorbed into the English; Hebrew in Kircher dropped; Yoruba tone marks and Hebrew vowel points lost.
classes.instrument: None. The audit counts the languages on a page but not whether each survives.

classes.name: Page furniture mis-tagged
classes.sees: The running head as the first sentence or as a heading; the catchword as the page's last word and translated; a page number read from show-through, a mount number or a chapter number.
classes.instrument: A page-number check against the book's own pagination (added after the study). Running heads, catchwords and signatures are not checked, and our page-integrity detectors read these tags as facts.

classes.name: Marginalia and apparatus dropped, merged or mis-tagged
classes.sees: A marginal note dropped or merged into the body; a body paragraph tagged as a margin note; a footnote number at a line-end hyphen taken as a margin note, so the split word is doubled.
classes.instrument: None.

classes.name: A later hand read as the text
classes.sees: A later reader's pencil marks tagged as insertions; ink doodles given a doctrinal meaning; a library stamp called a printer's mark.
classes.instrument: None.

classes.name: Labels and notation described, not transcribed
classes.sees: The forty Latin labels on a plate exist only inside a paraphrase, unsearchable and unquotable; a staff of music replaced by "[Diagram showing a musical cadence.]".
classes.instrument: None.

classes.name: Reasoning and page descriptions inside the transcription
classes.sees: "I am transcribing the right-hand page", "The image is a photograph of a manuscript page, likely from…", inside the text.
classes.instrument: A reasoning-leak check and a described-page check; the form wrapped in a metadata tag is not counted.

classes.name: The model's own page tags are wrong
classes.sees: French on a half-Syriac page; "Greek" and "Ancient Greek" on facing pages; two columns on a one-column page; an illustration type on a text page.
classes.instrument: None at page level; book-level language checks exist.

classes.name: Table structure invented or lost
classes.sees: A marginal keyword index fused with the body into a table; a single list doubled into two identical columns; a paradigm's cells scrambled; a row too long, so its last cell is not shown.
classes.instrument: None. A table check (ragged rows, duplicate cells) is free and not built.

classes.name: Translation cut short
classes.sees: The English stops a third of the way down the page, or mid-word ("with water and s").
classes.instrument: Length-ratio check in the page-integrity audit.

classes.name: Source left untranslated
classes.sees: The original left in place of the English (here, one word on one page).
classes.instrument: Echoed-source check in the page-integrity audit.

classes.name: Translation hidden inside a metadata tag
classes.sees: An empty or near-empty page. The translation exists, but it was written inside a metadata tag, and the renderer moves it out of the reading text.
classes.instrument: New translations are unwrapped at write time (added after the study). A length check reads existing cases as truncation, which implies the wrong repair.

classes.name: A page's last section moved to the next page
classes.sees: Page N's last section is missing from N and prepended to N+1, so every word is translated somewhere and no completeness check fails.
classes.instrument: Block-drift check (about 3% of in-block boundaries).

classes.name: The next page's opening translated twice
classes.sees: The next page's first clause finished at the end of this page and repeated at the start of the next; the catchword translated twice.
classes.instrument: Page-boundary audit of translations.

classes.name: Catchwords and split words at the break
classes.sees: At the break, a negation lost, a split word misjoined into another word, a syllable doubled, or an invented word or ellipsis to bridge a sentence whose verb is on the next page.
classes.seenNote: About 30 of 78 breaks had a defect of some kind; 4 more could not be judged because both sides were invented.
classes.instrument: Catchword checks in the page-integrity audit; a seam-repair pass for batch translation is measured (#5103).

classes.name: Fluent English built on garbled source
classes.sees: Confident English built on gibberish, on lines the transcription itself marks unclear, on stubs of a facing-page strip, on a repetition loop. Or the inverse: a word-by-word gloss shipped as the page.
classes.seenNote: This is the amplifier for the transcription classes above: the translator never declines.
classes.instrument: None. Withholding by default is the policy for whole scripts, not a page-level check.

examples.label: mDo sde brtags sna rgyas pa (Tibetan)

classes.name: Sense inverted or a qualifier dropped, with a correct transcription
classes.sees: Cold and hot drugs reversed; a negation dropped; "each guest fearing for his own life" becomes "fearing for the bridegroom's life".
classes.instrument: The monthly source-grounded judge of the quality study finds some, on one sampled page per book. Nothing runs on every page.

classes.name: Quiet omission in the translation
classes.sees: Five lines gone between two fluent sentences; a footnote dropped; a commentary replaced by a one-line note. Too small for a length check.
classes.instrument: A sentence-count check has been written (sentence-deficit.mjs) but does not yet run on the corpus.

classes.name: Invented scholarship in notes and glosses
classes.sees: Notes that explain a misread with confident, false learning: "Saint Rotoi (likely a reference to a local feast day)" where the leaf names St Christopher. The wrong reading arrives footnoted.
classes.instrument: None checks what a note says.

classes.name: Parallel edition mishandled
classes.sees: A smooth "translation of the Greek" that is really the editor's facing Latin, so his printed gaps vanish; a paraphrase of a printed facing English; both columns translated, so the reader gets two English versions.
classes.seenNote: Every parallel edition in the sample.
classes.instrument: None. Two source languages on most pages of a book is the free signal.

classes.name: English source rewritten into other English
classes.sees: Burton, Browne, Jonson "translated" into abridged, modernised English: "How Abu Hasan Brake Wind" becomes "Broke Wind", footnotes dropped, commentary condensed.
classes.seenNote: Nearly every English-source book in the sample. Editions after 1820 do not show this panel to readers.
classes.instrument: Since 30 September 2026 English pages are copied through, not paraphrased, for new translations. Existing paraphrases remain.

examples.label: Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 5

classes.name: Apparatus stripped in translation
classes.sees: Four of seven footnotes gone and the rest condensed with their attributions removed; an editor's emendation made meaningless; note numbers changed so the commentary no longer keys to the text.
classes.instrument: None measures whether notes survive.

classes.name: The two panes come from different reads
classes.sees: The English contains a passage the transcription lacks, translated from the image, from memory or from an earlier read; a translation five times the transcription's length.
classes.instrument: None asserts that the served English was made from the served transcription.

classes.name: Wrong "continues from previous page" notes
classes.sees: "Continues from previous page" at the start of a new section; a note about Coptic on a page with none; the previous page's English repeated inside the note.
classes.instrument: None.

classes.name: Form imposed or lost
classes.sees: Manuscript line breaks carried into English prose so it reads as broken verse; verse flattened to prose; running heads made into headings; invented "PAGE 85" headings.
classes.instrument: None.

classes.name: Markup the renderer does not know, or broken markup
classes.sees: Raw tags in the reading text (a signature, a page number, a column break); footnote keys written as HTML letters that collide with real tags; a margin note split by an orphan closing tag.
classes.seenNote: Readers checked the stored text, not the screen, except where noted.
classes.instrument: New translations are checked against the closed tag vocabulary at write time (added after the study). Existing pages are not.

classes.name: Metadata derived from bad text
classes.sees: Summaries, keywords and index entries derived from invented text: the Hebrew remedy book's summary describes divine unity.
classes.seenNote: Not counted; a consequence of every transcription class.
classes.instrument: None in this study.

classes.name: Our own measurements are wrong
classes.sees: A stored length of 108 characters for a page holding 8,100 lines of the character |; a translation length of zero for a page with a translation; strata that mostly were not what their tags said.
classes.seenNote: A finding about the sample, not counted per book.
classes.instrument: None. Every count in this paper is by eye for that reason.

specimens.title: The text of the page before
specimens.book: C. R. Day, The Music and Musical Instruments of Southern India and the Deccan (London, 1891), printed p. 63
specimens.alt: Head of a printed page: running title THE MUSIC OF SOUTHERN INDIA, page number 63, and the opening words with a major seventh
specimens.scan: Printed page 63. It opens "with a major seventh. A comparison of the examples he gives with songs of India…".

segs.text: <page-num>62</page-num> …
note in the middle of a roulade with which all Hindu music abounds. This is especially the case in the performance…
<page-num>63</page-num> … with a major seventh. A comparison of the examples he gives with songs of India will be of great interest…

specimens.note: Both records the readers checked carried the text of the page before their image. The transcription's own page number, 62, disagreed with the 63 printed on the scan, which is the cheapest tell. The page was read again from its image on 1 October 2026; the text shown is what was served until then.
specimens.servedOn: as served until 1 October 2026, from the page's revision history

specimens.title: Two manuscript pages in one frame
specimens.book: Hippocrates, Greek manuscript on microfilm (catalogued as a 1550 print), image 208
specimens.alt: A microfilm frame of an open Greek manuscript showing two full pages of minuscule script side by side
specimens.scan: A microfilm frame of an open codex: two full pages of Greek minuscule, side by side.

segs.text: <meta>The image shows a two-page spread of a Greek manuscript. I am transcribing the right-hand page (folio 109).</meta>
Συντείνειν δὲ πάνυ τὰ πρὸς τὰς ποίας ταύτας, ὥσπερ ἔφην, καὶ ὁ γελασμὸς τραχὺς δὲ γινόμενος…
Two records, one for each page, each transcribed in full.
The left page is in no record.

specimens.note: The model says what it is doing and does it: the left page is dropped, and the model's working note is stored inside the transcription (class O15). The readers of 25 September found only a few words of the right page's transcription on the leaf, so even the half that was kept is mostly confabulated (O1). The catalogue calls the book a print (I7).

specimens.title: Whole sentences built from line openings
specimens.book: Pierre Dupuy, Histoire de la condannation des Templiers (1713), printed p. 208
specimens.alt: Right edge of a printed Latin page beside a narrow strip of the facing page, which shows only the first two to four letters of each line
specimens.scan: On the right, the gutter and a strip of the facing page: only the first letters of each line, deti, poſ, quo, & p, qua, exig, libr, & c, Atq, plan, hab, mo, divi, hon, V, Ron, Epi.

segs.text: <column-break/> dent, sed in communi possident, ut in Monasteriis & per Ecclesias, quæ non sunt propriæ, sed exiguae… Atque hæc est Templariorum… Vota hæc, quæ Romani Pontifices & Episcopi exigebant, habebant in se, quod unusquisque in suo ordine & statu securus esset…
These vows, which the Roman Pontiffs and Bishops required, ensured that each man was secure in his own order and state…
Nothing. The strip is the edge of the facing page, whose full text is the next record. This page has one column.

specimens.note: The model fitted fluent, plausible Latin to the line openings, and the translation renders it as the Templars' rule. The reader then meets the real text of the facing page on the next record, so two versions of it are served, one invented. The transcription also tags this one-column page as two columns.

credit.text: Scan: Bibliotheca Philosophica Hermetica, Embassy of the Free Mind, Amsterdam. Public domain.

specimens.title: A treatise where the leaf has remedies
specimens.book: Sifre madaʿ segulot (Hebrew manuscript, 18th century), image 54
specimens.alt: Hebrew cursive manuscript: a short heading and the first numbered entry of a list, with a numeral in the right margin
specimens.scan: A heading, לחולי פצעים ("for those sick with sores"), then the first of the page's numbered entries, with its numeral in the right margin; the entry contains קח, "take".

segs.text: כי אם בעל פשוט יש בו האחדות גמורה ואינו מורכב כלל לא מחלקים ולא ממאוחרים…
For if the Master is simple, there is in Him absolute unity. He is not composed at all, not of parts, nor of "later" and "earlier"…
A list of numbered remedies for sores. None of the served text is on this leaf.

specimens.note: The served page is a philosophical treatise on divine simplicity, with numbered sections that mimic the leaf's numbered entries. The English translates it faithfully and the page summary repeats it. Each step is faithful to the one before, so nothing downstream objects. On the next leaf, also remedies, the readers of 25 September found the Yom Kippur confession served.

specimens.title: The printed prayer book's word, not the scribe's
specimens.book: Pocket-size Jewish prayer book (Hebrew manuscript, 15th–16th century), image 334
specimens.alt: Four lines of Hebrew semi-square script from the Unetanneh Tokef
specimens.scan: Lines 3–4 read ברעש ומי במגפה מי בדבר ומי ב / ברעב: by earthquake, by plague, by pestilence, by famine.

segs.text: ברעש ומי במגפה מי בדבר ומי ב ברעב
who by earthquake and who by plague,
who by pestilence and
who by famine
and who by drought
who by earthquake and who by plague, who by pestilence and who by famine

specimens.note: The transcription is right. The English drops the scribe's pestilence (בדבר) and adds drought, which is in the printed liturgy the model remembers, not in this manuscript. A manuscript's variants are why a reader opens it.

credit.text: Scan: John Rylands Library, University of Manchester (MS Gaster Hebrew 144). CC BY-NC 3.0.

specimens.title: One phrase, over and over
specimens.book: Tiḳun sheṭarot (Hebrew manuscript, late 18th–early 19th century), image 127
specimens.alt: The last eight lines of a dense Hebrew cursive page, each line different
specimens.scan: The last eight lines of the leaf, in a dense cursive hand. Every line is different.

segs.text: ובזה סוד שכינה וסוד שכינה / ובזה סוד שכינה וסוד שכינה / ובזה סוד שכינה וסוד שכינה / ובזה סוד שכינה וסוד שכינה / ובזה סוד שכינה וסוד שכינה
…and in this the secret of the Shekhinah and the secret of the Shekhinah…
A transcription of the leaf's own lines. The book is a formulary of legal deeds; the readers could match practically nothing of the served text to the leaf.

specimens.note: The transcription collapses into "the secret of the Shekhinah" and "the gate of understanding" and ends with one line five times. Its own note calls the page a kabbalistic treatise. The English translates every repetition, about 3,500 characters on this page, and nothing between the two steps notices a loop.

specimens.title: A line and a half dropped, the halves joined
specimens.book: Athanasius Kircher, Mundus subterraneus, vol. II (1678), printed p. 301
specimens.alt: Top of the right column of a printed Latin page, in italic and roman type, on a herb that turns metals into gold
specimens.scan: "…& lac habet in-|ſtar croci (Chelidoniam ego interpretor). Accipe ſuccum de hac herba & pone ſuper argen-|tum, & fiet cuprum."

segs.text: Caulem habet rubrum, & violaceum, & lac habet in
ſtar croci (Chelidoniam ego interpretor). Accipe ſuccum de hac herba & pone ſuper argen
tum, & fiet cuprum.
It has a red and violet stalk, and it has milk
within
, and it will become copper.
It has a red and violet stalk, and a milk like saffron (I take it to be celandine). Take the juice of this herb and put it on silver, and it will become copper.

specimens.note: The reading skips from in- to -tum and makes one word of the two halves. The English then makes a sentence of the join, and milk becomes copper. Nothing marks the gap. Earlier on the same page the transcription also drops vivum from argentum vivum, so quicksilver becomes silver.
